title: Variance basics: in, out, and assignability
hook: Variance answers: if Dog extends Animal, is Box<Dog> assignable to Box<Animal>? TypeScript uses structural rules — function parameters are contravariant, returns covariant, and readonly arrays are covariant in their element type.

blocks.text: **Covariance**: if `Dog extends Animal`, then `Producer<Dog>` can substitute where `Producer<Animal>` is expected — `T` appears only in **output** positions. **Contravariance**: `Consumer<Animal>` substitutes for `Consumer<Dog>` — `T` only in **input** positions. **Invariance**: neither direction is safe — `MutableArray<Dog>` is not `MutableArray<Animal>`. TypeScript checks **structural** positions: function return types are covariant; parameter types are contravariant (with strictFunctionTypes). **in/out** modifiers (TS 4.7+) on type parameters document variance explicitly.

entries.plainDefinition: Subtype of T implies subtype of Container<T> — T in output only.
entries.example: readonly Dog[] assignable to readonly Animal[]

entries.plainDefinition: Supertype of T accepted where subtype expected — T in input only.
entries.example: (animal: Animal) => void assignable to (dog: Dog) => void

entries.plainDefinition: TS 4.7+ explicit variance on interface type params.

blocks.text: Variance bugs cause runtime errors in collections — pushing a Cat into `Animal[]` that is actually `Dog[]`. Event handler typing relies on contravariance — `(e: Event) => void` accepts handlers for subtypes. C# has `in T` and `out T` on interfaces (`IEnumerable<out T>`, `IComparer<in T>`) enforced by CLR. TypeScript's rules are subtler because structural typing checks every member position. Senior interviews ask about `strictFunctionTypes`, readonly array covariance, and why `Array<Dog>` is not `Array<Animal>`.

blocks.title: PEP 484 mnemonic
blocks.body: Parameters are contravariant (flip direction). Returns are covariant (same direction).

diagram.title: Variance directions
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  DOG[Dog subtype Animal] --> COV["out T: same direction"]
  DOG --> CONTRA["in T: flip direction"]
  COV --> R[Return position]
  CONTRA --> P[Parameter position]

snippet.label: Mutable array invariance
snippet.explanation: Line 6: mutable Dog[] not assignable to Animal[] — could push Cat. Lines 8-9: readonly prevents writes — covariance safe.

snippet.label: Function parameter contravariance
snippet.explanation: Line 5: Handler<Animal> usable as Handler<Dog> — function accepts wider Animal, safe for Dog calls. Reverse fails — would assume Dog fields.

snippet.label: Explicit out/in modifiers (TS 4.7+)
snippet.explanation: out T — T only in output. Producer<Dog> assignable to Producer<Animal>. in T flips for input-only positions.

snippet.label: Failure mode — unsound cast through any
snippet.explanation: Cast bypasses compile-time invariance check — classic heap pollution bug. Never cast mutable arrays to wider element type.

blocks.title: Assuming arrays are covariant
blocks.body: Only readonly arrays are covariant — mutable Dog[] is not Animal[].

blocks.title: Disabling strictFunctionTypes
blocks.body: Without it, function parameter variance checks are unsound.

blocks.text: Bivariant methods on classes (pre-strict) caused soundness holes — strictFunctionTypes fixes function types only. `Method` bivariance still exists for class methods in some cases. Conditional types and infer preserve variance in mapped outputs. Library authors marking `Producer<out T>` document intent and get better error messages. LeetCode/Reddit: explain the push-to-Animal[]-that-is-Dog[] failure scenario.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Says all generics are covariant. Cannot explain Dog[] vs Animal[]. Unaware of strictFunctionTypes.

interviewTakeaways: Covariant: subtype flows same direction (returns, readonly out).
Contravariant: parameters flip direction — Handler<Animal> assignable to Handler<Dog>.
Mutable arrays invariant — readonly arrays covariant.
60s: Variance = assignability of generic types under subtyping. Params contravariant, returns covariant. Dog[] not Animal[] but readonly Dog[] ok. in/out modifiers document intent.
Follow-up: strictFunctionTypes, bivariant method caveat, C# IEnumerable<out T>.
commonPitfalls: Weak: "generics are always covariant" — rejected with Dog[] example.
Casting Dog[] to Animal[] for convenience.
Strong: "Check T positions. Mutable invariant, readonly covariant. Function params contravariant."

jsTsCorrelations.note: JS allows pushing any value into arrays — TS invariance on mutable arrays prevents compile-time unsound assignments.
C# IEnumerable<out T> is covariant by declaration; TS achieves similar via readonly T[] without runtime IEnumerable.
